THIS APPEAL HAVING BEEN HEARD AND RESERVED FOR JUDGMENT ON 12.07.2024 COMING FOR PRONOUNCEMENT OF JUDGMENT THIS DAY, THIS COURT DELIVERED THE FOLLOWING:
CORAM: THE HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE S.RACHAIAH  CAV JUDGMENT (PER: THE HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE S.RACHAIAH)
1.

This appeal is filed by the appellants being aggrieved by the judgment of conviction and order on sentence dated 21.10.2022 passed in Sessions Case No.136/2019 on the file of the I Additional District and Sessions Judge at Bagalkot, Sitting at Jamkhandi wherein the Trial Court convicted the accused Nos.1 and 2/appellants herein for the offences punishable under Section 489-D r/w Section 34 of Indian Penal Code (for short 'IPC').
2. The rank of the parties, henceforth, will be referred to as their rankings in the Trial Court, for convenience.

sentences.text:
Brief facts of the case:
3.

It is the case of the prosecution that on 20.11.2018, P.W.1 said to have received a credible information regarding counterfeiting currency notes which was being NC: 2024:KHC-D:14875 generated from the house of accused No.1 which is situated at Kadapatti Village of Jamakhandi Taluk.
4. P.W.1 along with his staff went to the place where it is alleged that accused Nos.1 and 2 were counterfeiting the currency notes.
P.W.1 saw that accused Nos.1 and 2 were indulging in counterfeiting of fake currencies.
Further, it is stated that the accused Nos.1 and 2 were cutting the paper to the currency size and heaping up the papers to counterfeit the currency notes.

5. P.W.1 and his staff immediately conducted a raid and seized the materials relating to the counterfeiting the currency notes and arrested the accused and thereafter, registered a case in Crime No.217/2018 for the offence stated supra.
After conducting the investigation, submitted the charge sheet.
6. The prosecution in order to prove its case, examined 4 witnesses as PWs.1 to 4 and got marked 12 documents as per Exs.P1 to 12 and also identified seven documents as M.Os.1 to 7.

The Trial Court after considering both oral and documentary evidence on record, opined that NC:
Suvarna D/O. Sidaramayya Mathad vs The State Of Karnataka on 9 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/125970985/
2 2024:KHC-D:14875 the appellants had committed the offences stated supra and recorded the conviction.
7. Heard Sri.Santhosh B. Malagoudar, learned counsel for the appellants and Sri.Praveena Y.
Devareddiyavara, learned High Court Government Pleader for respondent- State.
8.

entities.text: Suvarna D/O. Sidaramayya Mathad vs The State Of Karnataka on 9 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is the submission of the learned counsel for appellants that the judgment of conviction and order on sentence passed by the Court below is contrary to the evidence on record and opposed to the facts and circumstances of the case.
Therefore, the same is liable to be set aside.
9. It is further submitted that P.W.1 ought to have registered a case upon receiving a credible information relating to the cognizable offences.
However, P.W.1 proceeded to the spot without registering the FIR which is contrary to the settled principles of law.
Therefore, the judgment of conviction cannot be sustained.
10. It is further submitted that the Trial Court acted upon the evidence of official witnesses without being corroboration NC: 2024:KHC-D:14875 which is erroneous and not proper.
P.W.2 has been examined as panch witness to the seizure mahazar under which recovery of M.Os.1 to 7 is said to have taken place.
However, he has turned hostile and not supported the case.

11. It is further submitted that P.W.1 even though deposed in his evidence that he had seized some chemicals at the place of conducting search and seizure, the said chemical was not sent for chemical examination by the competent authority.
In the absence of a report relating to the chemical that can be used for counterfeiting the currency notes, it cannot be said that the prosecution has proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
In spite of many lacunae in the evidence, the Trial Court recorded the conviction which is erroneous and liable to be set aside.
Making such submissions, learned counsel for appellants prays to allow the appeal.
12. Per contra, the learned High Court Government Pleader for the State vehemently justified the judgment of conviction passed by the Trial Court.

Further, he NC: 2024:KHC-D:14875 submitted that the evidence of all the witnesses is consistent in respect of the search and seizure conducted by the respondent / Police and also consistent in their evidence regarding the arrest of accused Nos.1 and 2.
13.

It is further submitted that the respondent / Police have seized 414 black colour paper slips which resembles Rs.2,000/- currency note and also seized 414 black colour paper slips which resembles Rs.500/- currency note.
Further, it is submitted that the Investigating Officer and his team seized other machineries used for counterfeiting the currency notes.
14. It is further submitted that the accused / appellants did not explain in their statements as to how these documents have been found in their house.
In the absence of an explanation relating to the material objects, it cannot be said that the accused were not using those materials in counterfeiting the currency notes.

sentences.text: It is further submitted that the Trial Court rightly appreciated the evidence and documents on record and recorded the conviction which is appropriate and proper.
Therefore, interference with the said findings may not be necessary.

Making such submissions, the learned High Court Government Pleader prays to dismiss the appeal.
16.

After having heard the learned counsel for the respective parties and also perused the findings of the Trial Court in recording the conviction, it is relevant to refer to Section 489-D of IPC which reads as under:-
"Section 489D:- Making or possessing instruments or materials for forging or counterfeiting currency notes or bank- notes Whoever makes, or performs any part of the process of making, or buys of sells or disposes of, or has in his possession, any machinery, instrument of material for the purpose of being used, or knowing or having reason to believe that it is intended to be used, for forging or counterfeiting any currency-note or bank-note, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years,
and shall also be liable to fine."
The above said provision deals with counterfeiting currency notes or bank notes.

It starts with the definition that, whoever makes, or performs any part of the process of making, or buys or sells or disposes of, or has in his NC: 2024:KHC-D:14875 possession, any machinery, instrument of material for the purpose of making counterfeit currency notes shall be punished under the above-said provision.
17.

In the present case, a complaint has been filed by P.W.1 who was working as PSI of respondent /
Police.
The said complaint was lodged on 20.11.2018.
According to him, he stated to have received an information regarding preparing the counterfeit currency notes in the house of accused No.1.

After receiving the said information, he stated to have secured the presence of panch witnesses and also his staff, went to the house of accused No.1 and conducted the raid and also seized some material objects and also arrested the accused and thereafter, a complaint came to be registered by him before the Assistant Sub- Inspector of Police.
The Assistant Sub-Inspector of Police registered a case in Crime No.217/2018 for the offences punishable under Sections 489-D, 420, 511 r/w 34 of IPC.
After conducting the investigation, submitted charge sheet.

P.W.1 who was working as PSI of respondent - Police has stated in his evidence that he has seized the money counting machine of Maxwell Company, Samsung Xerox machine, small colour printer of Epson Company, four glass bottles containing chemicals and other related items which were in possession of accused Nos.1 and 2.
Though he was cross-examined by the defence and some suggestions were made

that the material objects alleged to have been seized by the respondent - Police in the house of P.W.1, the independent witness has not supported the case of the prosecution regarding the seizure of materials.

sentences.text: It is further noted that P.W.1 admitted in his cross- examination that the chemicals found in the bottles were not sent to FSL for chemical analysis.
P.W.1 further admitted that prior to conducting the raid, complaint and FIR were not registered.
20. P.W.2 was working as a Village Accountant.
He stated to have been called by P.W.1 to assist him in conducting the raid as a panch witness.
He has supported in his - 10 - NC: 2024:KHC-D:14875 evidence relating to the seizure of material objects in the house of accused No.1.

In the cross-examination, he has admitted that he was not aware about the house number where the material objects were recovered and also admitted that he was working at Taluk Office on the date of raid conducted and no movement register was maintained in the office.
Further, he has admitted that he affixed his signature to the said panchanama at the police station.

According to him, he has affixed his signature in the police station around 9.30 p.m.
21.
P.W.3 was working as Head Constable and is said to have accompanied P.W.1 in conducting the raid.
22. P.W.4 was working as C.P.I. of the said jurisdiction.
He stated to have conducted the investigation and submitted charge sheet.

23. Learned counsel for appellants raised a ground that FIR must be registered before conducting the search and seizure and it is mandatory in cases where an information relating to the commission of the cognizable offence.

Further, he submitted that as P.W.1 admitted in - 11 - NC: 2024:KHC-D:14875 his cross-examination that before conducting the raid, no FIR was registered to proceed to the spot which is contrary to the law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court.

24. In this context, it is relevant to refer the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of LALITHA KUMARI v. STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH1 wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court held in paragraph No.120 as follows:
"120.

entities.text: LALITHA KUMARI v. STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH1
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In view of the aforesaid discussion, we hold:
120.1.
The registration of FIR is mandatory under Section 154 of the Code, if the information discloses commission of a cognizable offence and no preliminary inquiry is permissible in such a situation.

Suvarna D/O. Sidaramayya Mathad vs The State Of Karnataka on 9 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/125970985/
5 120.2.

entities.text: Suvarna D/O. Sidaramayya Mathad vs The State Of Karnataka on 9 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: If the information received does not disclose a cognizable offence but indicates the necessity for an inquiry, a preliminary inquiry may be conducted only to ascertain whether cognizable offence is disclosed or not.
If the inquiry discloses the commission of a cognizable offence, the FIR must be registered.

In cases where AIR 2014 SC 187 : (2014) 2 SCC 1 - 12 - NC: 2024:KHC-D:14875 preliminary inquiry ends in closing the complaint, a copy of the entry of such closure must be supplied to the first informant forthwith and not later than one week.
It must disclose reasons in brief for closing the complaint and not proceeding further.
120.4. The police officer cannot avoid his duty of registering offence if cognizable offence is disclosed.
Action must be taken against erring officers who do not register the FIR if information received by him discloses a cognizable offence.
The scope of preliminary inquiry is not to verify the veracity or otherwise of the information received but only to ascertain whether the information reveals any cognizable offence.
As to what type and in which cases preliminary inquiry is to be conducted will depend on the facts and circumstances of each case.

The category of cases in which preliminary inquiry may be made are as under:
(a) Matrimonial disputes/family disputes (b) Commercial offences (c) Medical negligence cases (d) Corruption cases - 13 - NC: 2024:KHC-D:14875 (e) Cases where there is abnormal delay/laches in initiating criminal prosecution, for example, over 3 months' delay in reporting the matter without satisfactorily explaining the reasons for delay.
The aforesaid are only illustrations and not exhaustive of all conditions which may warrant preliminary inquiry.

120.7 [Ed.: This correction is based on para 120.7 as corrected vide order in Lalita Kumari v. State of U.P., (2023) 9 SCC 695.] . 6 complainant, a preliminary inquiry should be made time-bound and in any case it should not exceed fifteen days generally and in exceptional cases, by giving adequate reasons, six weeks' time is provided.

sentences.text: The fact of such delay and the causes of it must be reflected in the General Diary entry.

Since the General Diary/Station Diary/Daily Diary is the record of all information received in a police station, we direct that all information relating to cognizable offences, whether resulting in registration of FIR or leading to an inquiry, must be mandatorily and meticulously - 14 - NC: 2024:KHC-D:14875 reflected in the said diary and the decision to conduct a preliminary inquiry must also be reflected, as mentioned above.

"
25. On careful reading of the above said dictum of Hon'ble Supreme Court, the main object from the informant's point of view is to set the criminal law into motion and from the point of view of the Investigating Authority, to obtain information about alleged criminal activity, to be able to take suitable steps to trace and to bring book the guilty.

26. After having considered the principles laid down in the above said dictum and also considered that P.W.1 has admitted in his cross-examination that he had not registered any FIR before conducting the search and seizure, I am of the considered opinion that the Trial Court has committed an error in arriving at a conclusion that the prosecution has proved the case beyond all reasonable doubt and further, I am of the considered opinion that the appreciation of the evidence by the Trial Court is contrary to the settled principle of law.
Hence, the same is liable to be set aside.

. In the light of the observations made above, I proceed to pass the following:
ORDER i) The Criminal Appeal is allowed.
ii) The impugned judgment of conviction and order on sentence dated 21.10.2022 in Sessions Case No.136/2019 on the file of the I Additional District and Sessions Judge,
Bagalkot, Sitting at Jamkhandi, is set aside.
iii) The appellants / accused are acquitted for the offence under Section 489-D r/w 34 of IPC.
iv) The bail bond executed, if any, stands cancelled.
